stories.headline: NHL breakout tiers: Top players ready to level up in 2026-27
stories.summary: From players with new linemates to young stars set to hit superstardom to enticing rookies, watch out for this group.
stories.body:
One thing became clear when compiling our NHL breakout tiers for the 2026-27 season: The future is extraordinarily bright.

Like staring at the exposed bulb of a powerful floor lamp. Like opening up the blackout curtains straight into the morning sun. That kind of bright.

This season features a deep rookie class that is poised to make an immediate impact, as well as a few dozen young players ready to make the leap to stardom.

But our tiers also honor a handful of veterans who should see their fortunes change thanks to new environments and linemates.

Here are 40 NHL players ready to break out in 2026-27, organized into tiers that explain the circumstances behind their potential emergence. Enjoy!

Jump to a tier:

New scenery

Young star to superstar

The wait is over

Goalie breakouts

Rookie sensations

Tier 1: New scenery
These players switched teams and could see their profile rise with new scenery.

Bowen Byram

D, Chicago Blackhawks
It was a pretty simple equation. Byram was tied for 10th in 5-on-5 points (63) over the past two seasons among all defensemen. He was 63rd in power-play points (nine) in that same span, with the 48th highest ice time with the man advantage, taking second-unit minutes on the Buffalo Sabres behind Rasmus Dahlin.

So he goes to Chicago and gets to quarterback the top unit on a team that'll allow him to put the pedal down offensively, no matter his defensive issues, at even strength. He obliterates his career high in points (42) and begins to justify his $12.5 million cap hit beginning next season. You know ... theoretically.

John Carlson

D, Tampa Bay Lightning
This is an old star with a chance to be reignited. Carlson getting to run point on the Lightning power play gives the 36-year-old defenseman his greatest collection of offensive weaponry since the apex of Ovechkin-Backstrom-Kuznetsov man advantages. He had 60 points in 71 games last season, with just 14 points on the power play.

Luke Evangelista

RW, New Jersey Devils
One of GM Sunny Mehta's first big swings looks like a hit. The 24-year-old has been buzzing at 5-on-5 and contributing on the power play, adding some persistence and a net-front presence to a team that needed more of it. He's a staple in the Devils' top six already.

Hendrix Lapierre

C, Pittsburgh Penguins
We've been holding onto our Hendrix Lapierre stock for a while. The 24-year-old forward bounced between Washington and Hershey for a few years before ending up in Pittsburgh. He's played on Sidney Crosby's line and seems to have a fan in coach Dan Muse, who recently called the tenacious center/wing a "Swiss Army knife" player.

Devon Levi

G, Edmonton Oilers
The former Sabres goalie of the future is off to a 3-0-0 start for the rolling Oilers. Granted, his .863 save percentage, 3.35 goals-against average and negative goals saved above expected aren't great, but they're also not Tristan Jarry. Could Levi be the goalie Connor McDavid has been waiting for?

Kirill Marchenko

LW, Toronto Maple Leafs
Marchenko has already had an impact in the NHL, leading the Columbus Blue Jackets in goals for three straight seasons and amassing 103 tallies in his first 296 games. But he never had a superstar like Auston Matthews as his center. Marchenko breaking into point-per-game territory isn't too far a reach.

Mason McTavish

C, St. Louis Blues
"What happened to Mason McTavish?" was a common question among NHL fans who had previously watched him dominate junior hockey. There's no question the interruption to his training camp last season due to a contract dispute impacted his season in Anaheim. But overall, he hasn't popped like other young Ducks stars have. Perhaps a fresh start in St. Louis reignites his offensive game.

JJ Peterka

RW, Boston Bruins
Even with 25 goals last season, Peterka's time with the Utah Mammoth was frustrating for both player and team. Now he's back in the Eastern Conference and skating on the Bruins' second line behind David Pastrnak -- although he's getting a taste of Pasta on the power play.

Mackie Samoskevich

RW, Seattle Kraken

The Kraken sent a first- and a second-round pick to the Panthers for the 24-year-old winger buried on their depth chart, and then signed him to a three-year deal. Does more ice time -- and a spot next to Michigan teammate Matty Beniers -- help Samoskevich level up? Or is this just another middle-six forward for a franchise that seems to collect them like Pokémon?

Tier 2: Young star to superstar
You might already know these names. Get ready to hear them a lot more.

Jackson Blake

RW, Carolina Hurricanes
Blake's line with Logan Stankoven and Taylor Hall was the offensive engine for the Hurricanes before Jordan Staal decided to start scoring like Eric Staal in the Stanley Cup Final. Of the three, the 23-year-old Blake is the one who hasn't necessarily received the attention he deserves despite 22 goals last season and 20 points in 19 playoff games. That changes this season.

Quinton Byfield

C, Los Angeles Kings
The general vibe on Byfield this season is that if it's ever going to happen for him, it'll be with Artemi Panarin skating on his left side. The 24-year-old, selected No. 2 in 2020, has topped out at 24 goals and 55 points as career highs. If Panarin and other Kings wingers such as Adrian Kempe can't get him over those totals this season, who can?

Logan Cooley

C, Utah Mammoth
Cooley's breakout is just a matter of staying in the lineup. The 22-year-old center has been around nearly 3.00 points per 60 minutes over the past two seasons, and could have had his breakout last season were it for injuries that limited him to 54 games. A star in the making.

Ivan Demidov

RW, Montreal Canadiens
Demidov is the epitome of "young star to superstar." His 62 points in 82 games last season -- playing just 15:30 on average -- felt like just scratching the surface of his offensive game, especially if he ups his shots on goal.

Marco Rossi

C, Vancouver Canucks
My bold prediction before the season on the Canucks was that Rossi would find his game in Vancouver and become a No. 1 center. He has started strong with four points in four games. The problem is that he might end up thriving on the wing rather than at center. Well, it's a problem for me at least. I don't think the Canucks care where he scores, just that he does.

Beckett Sennecke

RW, Anaheim Ducks
Sennecke was third for the Calder last season behind Matthew Schaefer and Demidov after netting 23 goals for the Ducks. That was with one power-play goal and with an 11.7% shooting percentage. He has another gear in him, and his three goals through three games points to that.

Jimmy Snuggerud

RW, St. Louis Blues

A rookie last season, Snuggerud overcame a slow start to finish with a solid 51 points in 70 games. As long as he keeps his wagon hitched to center Robert Thomas, expect him to hit greater offensive heights this season.

Tier 3: The wait is over
Players we've been waiting to see break out who finally will.

Igor Chernyshov

LW, San Jose Sharks
The Sharks winger had 19 points in 28 games last season while spending a good chunk of the season in the AHL. Whether he hits that next level depends greatly on where he ends up in their lineup, as he spent copious time with Macklin Celebrini last season.

Tristan Luneau

D, Anaheim Ducks
Luneau is probably best known as the player who just signed a six-year, $43.2 million contract despite just 14 games played entering the season -- a symbol of GM Pat Verbeek's offer sheet paranoia. But people who knew the Ducks organization will tell you he has the goods. The more he plays with Jackson LaCombe, the better the chances are we'll get to see that.

Matvei Gridin

RW, Calgary Flames
The 20-year-old figures to be one of the bigger -- or only -- offensive threats on the rebuilding Flames. He had 30 points in 37 games last season, including 10 goals. As long as he still has scoring help on the roster in a continuing sell-off by the Flames, he should thrive.

Noah Ostlund

C, Buffalo Sabres
The 22-year-old Swede showed some strong potential as a No. 2 center last season, in particular clicking well with winger Zach Benson. If he can stay healthy -- an injury cut his postseason to just three games -- the Sabres could have a strong secondary scoring option behind Tage Thompson.

Gabe Perreault

RW, New York Rangers
The Rangers put the third-year winger out of Boston College in a position to break out, on the wing of Mika Zibanejad and Alexis Lafreniere. He's responded with a scoring start, scoring four points in five games. In the Rangers' retool -- or however they're defining it -- having Perreault become the kind of offensive force he was in college would be huge.

Vasily Podkolzin

RW, Edmonton Oilers
Here's a simple recipe for creating a breakout player: Take a winger who scored 19 goals, add either Connor McDavid or Leon Draisaitl (or both), and then watch that winger's stats inflate like a balloon. At least that's the hope with Podkolzin, who is playing on Edmonton's top line and top power-play unit.

Calum Ritchie

C, New York Islanders
Ritchie had a nice rookie season that was completely overshadowed by that other rookie's season in 2025-26. While he's no Matthew Schaefer, the 21-year-old picked up in the Brock Nelson trade two seasons ago is getting a push on the team's second line after 30 points in 65 games last season.

Matthew Wood

LW, Nashville Predators

The 21-year-old had 17 goals in 71 games last season playing all over the Nashville lineup, but he clicked best with star forward Filip Forsberg. They appear to have a good thing going on a line with Nils Hoglander at the start of the season, with Nashville expecting big things from Wood.

Tier 4: The goalie breakouts

Sebastian Cossa

Utah Mammoth
Cossa entered the season as the rookie backup to Karel Vejmelka, who logged an NHL-high 64 games last season. But when Cossa gets his chances, he'll be playing behind one of the better teams in the Western Conference, based on the early returns.

Nico Daws

New Jersey Devils
New GM Sunny Mehta put his full faith behind the 25-year-old German-born goaltender after the Devils traded Jacob Markstrom to the Panthers. He has played parts of four seasons with New Jersey but only nine games in the past two campaigns. This is his moment to take on an NHL job or leave the Devils to again search for a goalie solution.

Dylan Garand

New York Rangers
More than a few NHL observers were surprised that Garand, 24, made it through waivers before the Rangers recalled him to back up Igor Shesterkin. He has been stuck with Hartford in the AHL for four seasons but has played well enough that the Rangers might have to make a decision on veteran Joonas Korpisalo when he returns from injury.

Joel Hofer

St. Louis Blues
There was a time when having another St. Louis Blues goalie usurp Jordan Binnington as the starter seemed unlikely. But Hofer, 26, badly outplayed Binnington last season and was a key factor in the Blues' strong finish. He seems primed to join the ranks of dependable NHL starters.

Sergei Murashov

Pittsburgh Penguins
It's just a matter of time before the 22-year-old rookie netminder starts earning the majority of the starts for the Penguins, having dominated in the AHL and the KHL.

Clay Stevenson

Winnipeg Jets

What happens when a three-time Vezina Trophy winner demands a trade and then is suspended by his team? Well, that team needs to find itself another goalie or two.

The Jets brought in veteran Stuart Skinner but also made a waiver claim on Washington goalie Stevenson, a 27-year-old who has played mostly for Hershey. As long as Connor Hellebuyck doesn't return to the Winnipeg locker room, the talented Stevenson should get his most NHL ice time ever if he keeps earning it.

Tier 5: Rookie sensations
First-year players who aren't waiting for their breakout.

Viggo Bjorck

C, Winnipeg Jets
The No. 8 pick in June's draft, the Swedish center was earning second-line minutes early in the season but will have to produce offensively to keep that status.

Luca Cagnoni

D, San Jose Sharks
After two seasons putting up big offensive numbers with the AHL Barracuda, the 21-year-old made the Sharks out of camp and averaged over 20 minutes in ice time during his first three games, including top power-play unit duties. The diminutive (5-9) defenseman was a fourth-round pick in 2023. Can he handle the physical toll of big NHL minutes?

Anton Frondell

C, Chicago Blackhawks
After last season's appetizer -- nine points in 12 games after arriving from Djurgardens IF of the Swedish Hockey League -- Frondell is already showing he's going to cook this season. The No. 3 pick in 2025 had four points in his first four games, earning first-unit power-play time.

James Hagens

F, Boston Bruins
The Boston College product has run the rookie gamut early in the season: flashes of offensive spark and bouts of defensive befuddlement. But he'll improve.

Cole Hutson

D, Washington Capitals
The younger brother of Montreal star Lane Hutson, the 20-year-old had 10 points in 14 games last season and looks to be a key puck-mover on the Capitals' blue line this season while earning second-unity power-play minutes.

Roman Kantserov

RW, Chicago Blackhawks
Kantserov led the KHL with 36 goals last season as a 21-year-old winger before finally making the leap to the NHL. He's a great puck handler and a creative playmaker. Once he gets adjusted to the North American game, Kantserov has the skill set to be an offensive force.

Porter Martone

RW, Philadelphia Flyers
Like the rest of the Flyers, Martone has gotten out of the blocks slowly. But it's just a matter of time before the Martone we saw late last season -- a 19-year-old, playing like a 10-year veteran -- reemerges.

Gavin McKenna

LW, Toronto Maple Leafs
The No. 1 pick in June's draft got his first taste of the Toronto media pressure cooker after going scoreless in his first three NHL games. But McKenna accepted the challenge and calmed everyone down with a goal and an assist in a win over Nashville. He's skating next to John Tavares and William Nylander. He's positioned to thrive.

Ilya Protas

C, Washington Capitals
The young center is skating with brother Aliaksei and key offseason addition Jordan Kyrou on the Capitals' third line. It's a trio that could do some damage this season.

Ivar Stenberg

LW, San Jose Sharks
The No. 2 pick in June, Stenberg was slotted right onto the team's second line and top power-play unit. The sky's the limit for the 19-year-old Swede, provided he's ready.

stories.headline: Singapore Grand Prix 2026: Race start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions
stories.summary: Formula 1's original night race is back as drivers prepare for the ultimate challenge around the Marina Bay Circuit in Singapore.
stories.body:
Formula 1's original night race is back as drivers prepare for the ultimate challenge around the Marina Bay Circuit in Singapore.

It will also be the sixth and final sprint race of the season as Singapore hosts it for the first time.

Max Verstappen claimed his first victory of the season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, while Kimi Antonelli extended his lead in the title championship to 84 points from George Russell.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 17th round of the season.

- Bahrain GP was the worst indictment of F1's new engine regs yet

- Could Malaysia return to F1 calendar? The state of play despite Sepang travel chaos

- Max Verstappen wins disrupted Bahrain GP, Kimi Antonelli extends title lead as George Russell retires

Singapore Grand Prix schedule
All times in BST

Friday, October 9

Max Verstappen takes first pole for sprint race at Singapore Grand Prix following another settings issue

Saturday, October 10

Sprint: 10 a.m. - 11 a.m.

Qualifying: 2 p.m. - 3 p.m.

Sunday, October 11

Singapore Grand Prix: 1 p.m.

How to watch

Every practice and qualifying session as well as the race itself will be available to watch on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the Singapore Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Marina Bay Street Circuit

Singapore is one of the toughest challenges on the calendar for drivers due to the intense humidity and physically demanding nature of the circuit.

But this time round the drivers will have had a chance to get used to the humid conditions after racing in Malaysia for the Bahrain Grand Prix last weekend.

The Marina Bay Circuit has been on the calendar since 2008 and is one of the standout tracks. The race takes place at night with its breathtaking views of the city's skyline as cars make their way through the tight and twisty circuit.

Drivers can lose around 3kg in body weight after each race due to the amount they sweat.

Singapore Grand Prix

Circuit: Marina Bay Street Circuit; Singapore

Previous winners in Singapore

2014: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2015: Sebastian Vettel (Ferrari)

2016: Nico Rosberg (Mercedes)

2017: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2018: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2019: Sebastian Vettel (Ferrari)

2022: Sergio Pérez (Red Bull)

2023: Carlos Sainz (Ferrari)

2024: Lando Norris (McLaren)

2025: George Russell (Mercedes)

Other key stats

First F1 race: 2008

Lap record: 1:33.808 Lewis Hamilton (2025)

Most wins: Sebastian Vettel has the most wins with five (2011-2013, 2015 and 2019). From the current grid, Hamilton has four wins (2009, 2014, 2017-2018) and Fernando Alonso with two (2008 and 2010). Pérez (2022), Sainz (2023), Norris (2024) and Russell (2025) have all won a race each here.

Most poles: Vettel (2011, 2013, 2015, 2017) and Hamilton (2009, 2012, 2014, 2018) share the pole record with four each. From the current grid, Charles Leclerc (2019, 2022) has had two pole positions here.

Weather forecast

The weather for the Singapore Grand Prix is set to be thundery showers and light winds throughout the weekend, with highs of 34°C on Friday. The temperature is forecast to drop a degree for the remainder of the weekend.

What happened last time out?
Russell claimed pole position in Singapore last year and crossed the line 0.182 seconds clear of Red Bull's Verstappen, with McLaren's Oscar Piastri behind.

Russell took his second win of the season, but there was plenty of other drama during the race, especially at McLaren.

Norris, who started in fifth, knocked into Piastri when trying to pass him in the first corner. Piastri managed to gain some ground towards the end of the race, but he had to settle for fourth on the day McLaren lifted the trophy for the constructors' title.

Piastri's drivers' championship lead to Norris was separated by only 22 points with six races left of the season.

Who will win this year?

One to watch this weekend is Red Bull and Verstappen after he won the race last weekend. The team brought major upgrades two races ago and improvements to its overall performance has been evident.

Russell, who suffered a major blow to his championship hopes after retiring last time out, will be looking to maximise the points on offer across the weekend.

Mercedes are expected to be strong, while Ferrari are quick in cornering speed. Hamilton has won four times here, so could be a threat. McLaren's Norris and Piastri fell under the radar and struggled for pace in Malaysia.

All will be to play for under the lights in Singapore as we head into the business end of the season.

stories.headline: Saints AFLW coach steps down as club plans review
stories.summary: Embattled St Kilda AFLW coach Nick Dal Santo has stepped down amid the club's winless season.
stories.body:
Embattled St Kilda AFLW coach Nick Dal Santo has stepped down amid the club's winless season.

The last-placed Saints will conduct a review into their AFLW program, led by former Carlton football boss Brad Lloyd, in the wake of Dal Santo's departure.

Dal Santo, a St Kilda great as a player, was in his sixth season at the Saints and will coach his final game against Collingwood on Saturday, before departing.

"I've been giving a lot of thought to my future and whether continuing in this role was the right decision, both for myself and the program," Dal Santo said in a statement.

"Where we've been able to take this program is something I'll always be incredibly proud of.

"It's been a privilege to coach this group and help shape its formative years in the competition.

"I have a strong love for this club, I wanted to contribute to women's football, and with a daughter of my own, it's great to see a pathway for young females with football ambitions.

"I'm looking forward to finishing my time as coach alongside the group this weekend and wish them every success for what comes next."

The Saints will have three games left in the season after Saturday, when they will attempt to amend their unwanted record of being the only winless team in the competition.

"Nick has made a significant contribution to our AFLW program across six seasons and will always be an important part of our football club," St Kilda chief executive Carl Dilena said in a statement

"His care, commitment and leadership have been unwavering, and we thank him for everything he has given to the program, including leading the team to its maiden final's appearance last season.

"We look forward to recognising Nick's contribution this weekend as he leads the team one final time in front of our members and supporters at RSEA Park."

Lloyd will lead the review, via Apogee Sports, during the remainder of the season, while the Saints start their hunt for their next coach.

"Our ambition is to be a consistently competitive and respected club that can contend with the best in the competition," Dilena said.

"We want to give our AFLW program every chance to achieve this and that means identifying where we need to improve, investing in the right areas and acting with urgency."

stories.headline: Silva rises in P4P women's top 10, making most of golden opportunity
stories.summary: After winning UFC women's flyweight title, Silva rises in ESPN's P4P top 10.
stories.body:
The women's flyweight division might be the most stacked weight class in the UFC, and Natalia Silva wears the gold.

Silva was too fast, too precise and too elusive for Wang Cong in the UFC 332 main event on Saturday, and as a result, the 29-year-old from Brazil captured the vacant 125-pound title. She moves up one position to No. 4 in the ESPN women's pound-for-pound rankings.

Silva is one of seven flyweights in the women's top 10. The division with the next most pound-for-pound elites is lightweight, with three fighters in the men's rankings.

The top two fighters on the women's list are Valentina Shevchenko, who vacated the UFC title last month while healing shoulder and back injuries, and Zhang Weili, a two-time former strawweight titlist who last fought at flyweight, in an unsuccessful challenge of Shevchenko in November.

Aside from Silva, there are three other UFC flyweights in the top 10 (Alexa Grasso, Manon Fiorot and Erin Blanchfield), and the rankings also include PFL 125-pounder Dakota Ditcheva.

UFC women's bantamweight champion Kayla Harrison has been missing from these rankings for the past few months because, with no fights since June 2025, she is ineligible. But Harrison will return from neck surgery to defend her title against former two-division champion and consensus GOAT Amanda Nunes at UFC 334 on Nov. 14.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Oct. 7. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Valentina Shevchenko

UFC flyweight

Record: 26-4-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Zhang Weili, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

Shevchenko's dominance came under question in 2022 and 2023, when she went 1-1-1 in a trilogy with Alexa Grasso. Boy, does that feel like a long time ago now. Shevchenko more than reasserted herself as the best flyweight in the world, and then she established herself as the No. 1 woman in the world, period. It wasn't surprising that she beat Zhang, but it was surprising how easy she made it look. Shevchenko is out injured, however, so she has vacated her UFC title, which Natalia Silva captured by beating Wang Cong at UFC 332. When Shevchenko is healed up, she'll be looking to take back the belt.

2. Zhang Weili

UFC flyweight / strawweight

Record: 26-4

Last: L (UD) vs. Valentina Shevchenko, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

It's hard to move up in weight, especially at the highest level. That sounds like it should be obvious, but Zhang had been dominant at 115 pounds for so long, some of us might have taken for granted how big of a challenge moving to 125 would be. UFC 322 was a bad night for Zhang, but she doesn't have many. And if she decides to stay at flyweight, it certainly seems reasonable to believe she'll fare better in the future.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight champion

Previous ranking: 5

Record: 21-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Wang Cong, Oct. 3

Next: TBA

Silva was looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Rose Namajunas at UFC 324. And now she has fulfilled that expectation, beating Wang at UFC 332 to win the belt vacated by injured Valentina Shevchenko. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027.

5. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Previous ranking: 4

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

8. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

9. Erin Blanchfield

UFC flyweight

Record: 14-2

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Tracy Cortez, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: Oct. 17 vs. Jasmine Jasudavicius

Her rise toward the top of the division was derailed by a March 2024 loss to Manon Fiorot, but Blanchfield bounced back with two straight wins, including one over two-time former strawweight champion Rose Namajunas in November 2024. If she wins her upcoming bout with Jasudavicius, a fellow top-10 flyweight contender, Blanchfield would inch ever closer to a title shot.

10. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Record: 12-1

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Loopy Godínez, April 11

Next: TBA

If Suarez is still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Godinez, a fellow top-10 strawweight. Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Valentina Shevchenko; 2. Zhang Weili; 3. Mackenzie Dern; 4. Natalia Silva; 5. Cris Cyborg; 6. Alexa Grasso; 7. Manon Fiorot; 8. Dakota Ditcheva; 9. Erin Blanchfield; 10. Tatiana Suarez.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Cyborg; 3. Silva; 4. Zhang; 5. Dern; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Suarez; 9. Fiorot; 10. Blanchfield.

Andrew Davis: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Dern; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Fiorot; 9. Blanchfield; 10. Suarez.

Dre Waters: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Dern; 5. Silva; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Blanchfield; 9. Fiorot; 10. Suarez.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Grasso; 6. Dern; 7. Fiorot; 8. Blanchfield; 9. Suarez; 10. Ditcheva.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Record: 20-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Dvalishvili

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet. He can prove it by beating Dvalishvili again.

3. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Record: 21-5

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Yan

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. They will fight for a third time at UFC 333.

T-4. Tom Aspinall

UFC heavyweight

Record: 15-3, 1 NC

Last: NC1 vs. Ciryl Gane, Oct. 25, 2025

Next: TBA

You can make a case that Aspinall is the most dynamic, skillful, talented heavyweight the sport has seen. He is dominating opponents in a way that is unmatched. No one can last a round with him. He had hoped to prove his supremacy against Jon Jones, but Jones opted to retire, elevating Aspinall from interim champion. His first defense of the undisputed belt ended anticlimactically, as an eye poke resulted in his UFC 321 fight with Gane being declared a no-contest. Still recovering from the eye injury, Aspinall vacated his title on Sept. 14.

T-4. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

6. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

7. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Record: 28-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Diego Lopes, Jan. 31

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Movsar Evloev

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (38) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. Can he hand Evloev his first loss at UFC 333?

8. Joshua Van

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 18-2

Last: W (UD) vs. Alexandre Pantoja, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Van has been champion since December, but until UFC 331, there were doubters. Van had been handed the belt by default, when his challenge for the title was waved off after 26 seconds because Pantoja dislocated his left elbow. Van went on to defend the title against Tatsuro Taira in May, then faced Pantoja in a rematch at UFC 331. Van produced a clear victory -- his eighth win in a row -- to leave no doubt who rules at 125 pounds.

9. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight champion

Record: 14-2, 1 NC

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Alex Pereira, June 14

Next: Nov. 14 vs. Josh Hokit

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight on the White House lawn. Gane was elevated to undisputed champ after Aspinall, still injured, vacated his title, and the new champ will defend against Hokit at UFC 334.

10. Arman Tsarukyan

UFC lightweight

Record: 24-3

Last: W (KO1) vs. Mauricio Ruffy, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Tsarukyan is right back in the place he was in January 2025 -- on the cusp of a title fight. He withdrew from a challenge of Islam Makhachev one day before UFC 311 because of a back injury, and later in the year he was passed over twice when the UFC was booking lightweight title bouts. But by knocking out Ruffy with an elbow in the first round at UFC 331, Tsarukyan put himself back at the front of the line.

Other fighter receiving votes: Alex Pereira.

Brett Okamoto: 1. Islam Makhachev; 2. Petr Yan; 3. Merab Dvalishvili; 4. Ilia Topuria; 5. Alexander Volkanovski; 6. Joshua Van; 7. Arman Tsarukyan; 8. Ciryl Gane; 9. Alex Pereira; 10. Justin Gaethje.

Andrew Davis: 1. Makhachev; 2. Tom Aspinall; 3. Yan; 4. Dvalishvili; 5. Gaethje; 6. Topuria; 7. Volkanovski; 8. Van; 9. Gane; 10. Tsarukyan.

Dre Waters: 1. Makhachev; 2. Aspinall; 3. Yan; 4. Dvalishvili; 5. Gaethje; 6. Volkanovski; 7. Topuria; 8. Van; 9. Gane; 10. Pereira.

stories.headline: New Zealand Rugby launches legal action against ARLC over 'Chiefs' name
stories.summary: The battle over the use of the "Chiefs" name is headed to the New Zealand High Court after New Zealand Rugby launched legal action against the Australian Rugby League Commission.
stories.body:
The battle over the use of the "Chiefs" name is headed to the New Zealand High Court after New Zealand Rugby launched legal action against the Australian Rugby League Commission.

NZR on Thursday said it had been left with no choice but to launch legal proceedings against the ARLC, who has sought to adopt the name for its Papua New Guinea expansion franchise.

The PNG Chiefs are due to join the NRL in 2028 and have already signed a raft of players, including code-hoppers Zac Lomaz and Joey Manu, but they may yet have to undergo a chanGe of name if NZR gets its way.

The Chiefs' Super Rugby franchise has existed since 1996, with NZR claiming the introduction of the PNG Chiefs would result in "significant confusion and damage" should they be allowed to compete under the name from 2028.

"New Zealand Rugby (NZR) has today moved to protect the Chiefs brand and is filing proceedings in the High Court of New Zealand against the decision by the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) to launch a new NRL side using "Chiefs" in its name," an NZR statement read.  

"NZR is seeking both an interim and final injunction which stops the use of the names 'PNG Chiefs', 'Chiefs' or any other similar names in New Zealand.   

"The Chiefs have competed as a professional rugby team in Super Rugby since 1996 and over those 30 years, have built a strong identity and fanbase across New Zealand, Australia and internationally.  

"In New Zealand, NZR owns both the trademark rights for the word Chiefs and the Chiefs logo and since 1998, NZR has also held trademark protection for the Chiefs logo in Australia."

NZR claims it had tried to engage with the ARLC in an attempt to find a resolution, yet the commission was now intent on proceeding with the official launch of the PNG Chiefs on Oct. 21.

"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans," NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster said. "We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand.   

"We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific. We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."  

The Chiefs won two Super Rugby titles in back-to-back seasons in 2012 and 2013, and were runners-up in Super Rugby Pacific this season after suffering a crushing defeat by the Hurricanes in the decider.

The Hamilton-based team has produced countless All Blacks since its inception, with Saturday's run-on team to face the Wallabies featuring six players from the franchise.

"Here in New Zealand, when people hear 'the Chiefs', they think of this club and this region. The identity carries significant cultural meaning and connection to the region and its people, we know it means a great deal to our players and coaches past and present, fans and supporters here and around the world," Chiefs CEO Simon Graafhuis said.   

"Teams in different sports and markets can exist alongside one another with the same name, but the issue here is the similarity of our sports competing in the same market, for the same fans, in overlapping windows."  

However, ARLC executive chairman Peter V'Landys later issued a stinging rebuke, insisting he would vigorously defend PNG's right to use the Chiefs as its team name.

"The hypocrisy is mind-blowing, considering the Auckland Blues in 1996 used the NSW Blues name without any consultation or approval. The NSW Blues had been the Blues for in excess of 50 years before that," he said.

"Rugby union is obviously feeling threatened by rugby league in New Zealand, with sell-outs at most rugby league games."

No date has yet been slated for the hearing in New Zealand's High Court.
